chem_ocra.17.4.summary: Potable water is water that is safe for humans to drink because it has sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and microbes. The method used to produce potable water depends entirely on the source: freshwater is treated via filtration and chlorination, whereas seawater must undergo desalination via distillation or reverse osmosis. Understanding these processes, their energy requirements, and the distinction between pure water and potable water is essential for OCR Chemistry.

core.h: Definition of Potable Water
core.p: Potable water is not the same thing as pure water. In chemistry, pure water consists solely of H2O molecules with no dissolved substances whatsoever. Potable water, however, is simply water that is safe to drink.
bullets: Contains dissolved minerals and salts (such as calcium and magnesium ions)
Must have sufficiently low levels of dissolved microbes and pathogens
Must have low levels of toxic chemical substances
Does not need to be chemically pure to be safe for human consumption

callouts.p: Water that is safe for humans to drink.
Never write that potable water is pure water. Pure water contains only H2O and has a boiling point of exactly 100 degrees Celsius.

core.h: Sources of Water for Potable Supply
core.p: The availability of water varies dramatically across the globe depending on climate and geography. Water sources are generally categorised into freshwater and saltwater systems.
bullets: Freshwater sources include rivers, streams, lakes, and underground aquifers (groundwater)
Waste water (sewage and agricultural runoff) must also be treated before entering waterways
Seawater is an abundant resource in coastal areas but requires extensive treatment
The choice of water treatment depends entirely on the initial quality and source of the water

callouts.p: The methods used to produce potable water depend heavily on the available supplies of fresh water and local conditions.

core.h: Freshwater Treatment: Filtration
core.p: Rainwater collects in lakes and rivers, providing a relatively low-salt freshwater source. The first major stage of making this water potable is removing insoluble solid particles.
bullets: Water is passed through a wire mesh screen to catch large floating debris such as twigs and plastic
Bed filters made of fine sand and gravel layers are used to filter out smaller insoluble suspended particles
Coagulants like aluminium sulfate may be added to cause tiny suspended clay particles to clump together and settle out
Sedimentation tanks allow heavier particles to sink to the bottom as sludge

callouts.p: Filtration removes insoluble solids only. It does not remove dissolved salts or microscopic bacteria.

fig.cap: Diagram showing the passage of freshwater through a wire mesh screen followed by gravel and sand filter beds.

core.h: Freshwater Treatment: Sterilisation
core.p: Even after filtration removes all solid debris, water can still contain harmful microorganisms and bacteria that cause waterborne diseases such as cholera and typhoid.
bullets: Sterilisation kills microbes remaining in the water supply
Chlorine gas is commonly bubbled through the water to sterilise it
Ozone gas can also be used as a powerful oxidising agent to kill bacteria
Ultraviolet (UV) light can be shone through the water to destroy microbial DNA

callouts.p: Chlorine is added to potable water supplies specifically to kill microbes and harmful bacteria, making it safe from biological infection.

core.h: Desalination of Seawater: Overview
core.p: In areas where fresh water is extremely scarce (such as arid desert regions), countries must rely on extracting potable water from the oceans through desalination.
bullets: Desalination removes both dissolved salts and impurities from seawater
The two main methods used are thermal distillation and reverse osmosis
Both methods require very large amounts of electrical or thermal energy
High energy demands make desalinated water expensive to produce compared to freshwater treatment

callouts.p: Examiners frequently ask why desalination is not used everywhere. The key reason is the extremely high energy requirement and financial cost.

core.h: Desalination by Distillation
core.p: Thermal distillation mimics the natural water cycle by boiling liquid water into steam and then condensing that steam back into liquid water.
bullets: Seawater is heated until it boils, turning water into water vapour
Dissolved salts and minerals are left behind as solid residue in the boiling vessel
The water vapour travels into a condenser where it is cooled by cold water
The vapour condenses back into pure liquid water, which is collected in a separate container

callouts.p: Distillation requires heating large volumes of water to its boiling point (100 degrees Celsius), consuming vast amounts of fuel or electricity.

fig.cap: Simple distillation apparatus showing seawater being heated, vapor rising, condensing in a Liebig condenser, and pure water collected.

core.h: Desalination by Reverse Osmosis
core.p: Reverse osmosis is a membrane-based separation technique that forces water molecules through a semi-permeable membrane under high pressure.
bullets: Seawater is passed through a special semi-permeable membrane at very high pressure
The membrane has microscopic pores that are large enough to let water molecules pass through
The pores are too small for hydrated sodium and chloride ions (dissolved salts) to pass
Pure water is collected on the low-pressure side, leaving a concentrated brine solution behind

callouts.p: Reverse osmosis relies on membranes that selectively allow water molecules through while blocking dissolved salt ions.

core.h: Required Practical: Analysis and Purification of Water Samples
core.p: OCR specifies a required practical where students must test samples of water from different sources, determine their purity, and purify a sample using distillation.
bullets: Test pH of each water sample using universal indicator paper or a pH meter
Measure the mass of an empty evaporating basin using a sensitive analytical balance
Add a fixed volume of water sample to the basin and heat gently using a Bunsen burner until all water evaporates
Allow the basin to cool, re-weigh it, and calculate the mass of dissolved solid residue left behind
Perform a simple distillation to purify a salty or impure water sample

callouts.p: Mass of solid = (Mass of basin + solid) - (Mass of empty basin). Always record masses to the same number of decimal places.

core.h: Safety and Precautions in the Water Practical
core.p: Practical chemistry experiments involving heating equipment and electrical devices require rigorous adherence to safety protocols.
bullets: Wear eye protection (safety goggles) throughout the experiment
Take care when heating glassware to prevent spitting and boiling over
Allow apparatus to cool fully before attempting to touch or move glassware
Ensure electrical heating mantles or burners are positioned safely on heat-resistant mats

callouts.p: Hot glass looks identical to cold glass. Never pick up evaporating basins or boiling flasks immediately after heating.

core.h: Alternative Water Sources: Waste Water Treatment
core.p: In densely populated areas with limited rainfall, waste water from homes, agriculture, and industry must be treated to produce potable water or recycled water.
bullets: Sewage treatment involves screening to remove large objects and grit removal
Sedimentation produces sewage sludge and effluent
Anaerobic digestion breaks down the sewage sludge safely to produce biogas and fertilizer
Biological aerobic digestion treats the effluent to remove organic matter and harmful pathogens

callouts.p: Effluent is the liquid waste that undergoes aerobic biological treatment, while sludge is the solid semi-solid material that undergoes anaerobic digestion.

analogy.p:
Think of water treatment like processing passengers at airport security. Screening and sand filtration are like the metal detectors and bag scanners that remove bulky, unwanted items (large debris and insoluble grit). Sterilisation with chlorine is like checking passenger IDs to ensure no dangerous individuals slip through (killing microscopic pathogens). Desalination by reverse osmosis is like a VIP checkpoint with ultra-strict passport control that stops even the smallest individual passengers (dissolved salt ions) while letting others pass. 

Where the analogy breaks down: Airport security does not alter the physical state of the passengers, whereas distillation of seawater actively boils water into steam and condenses it back into a liquid, changing its physical state entirely.

terms.d: Water that is safe for humans to drink.
Water that contains only H2O molecules with zero dissolved solids or impurities.
The process of removing dissolved salts and minerals from seawater to produce fresh water.
A separation technique involving boiling a liquid to form a vapour and condensing that vapour back into a liquid.
A desalination process where water is forced under high pressure through a semi-permeable membrane.
The process of killing harmful microorganisms and bacteria using chemicals or UV light.
A separation method used to separate insoluble solid particles from a liquid using filter beds.
The process where suspended solid particles sink to the bottom of a container under gravity.
The liquid waste water remaining after initial sedimentation in sewage treatment.
The solid organic waste material collected at the bottom of sedimentation tanks during sewage treatment.
An underground layer of water-bearing permeable rock or gravel from which groundwater can be extracted.
A barrier with tiny microscopic pores that allows small molecules like water to pass through while blocking larger ions.

mistakes.r: Potable water contains dissolved minerals and salts. Pure water contains only H2O molecules.

mistakes.w: Filtration removes dissolved salts from water.
mistakes.r: Filtration only removes insoluble solid particles. Dissolved salts pass straight through filter paper and sand.

mistakes.w: Chlorine is added to water to make it taste nice.
mistakes.r: Chlorine is added specifically to kill harmful microorganisms and bacteria (sterilisation).

mistakes.w: Desalination is cheap and used everywhere.
mistakes.r: Desalination requires large amounts of energy and is expensive, so it is mainly used where freshwater is scarce.
Boiling kills bacteria and sterilises water, but any dissolved salts remain in the container when the water evaporates.

mistakes.w: Water from rivers is clean enough to drink straight away.
mistakes.r: River water contains untreated sewage, agricultural runoff, microbes, and pollutants, so it must be treated.

exam.q: Explain the difference between pure water and potable water.
model: Pure water contains only H2O molecules with no dissolved substances
Potable water is safe to drink and contains dissolved minerals and salts
exam.tip: Make sure you state that potable water contains dissolved substances whereas pure water does not.

exam.q: Describe how freshwater from a river is treated to make it potable.
model: Water is passed through a wire mesh screen to remove large debris
Filtration through sand and gravel beds removes insoluble solid particles
Chlorination or UV sterilisation kills harmful bacteria and microorganisms
exam.tip: List the three main stages in correct chronological order for full marks.

exam.q: Explain why seawater must be treated differently from freshwater before it is safe to drink.
model: Seawater contains very high concentrations of dissolved salts
Standard filtration and sterilisation do not remove dissolved ions, so desalination is required
exam.tip: Emphasise that dissolved salts are the key problem in seawater.

exam.q: Name two methods used for desalination of seawater.
model: Distillation
Reverse osmosis
exam.tip: Simply naming the two acceptable methods from the specification is sufficient.

exam.q: Explain why desalination is not used extensively in countries with abundant freshwater supplies.
model: Desalination requires very large amounts of energy
This makes the process expensive compared to treating local freshwater sources
exam.tip: Always link the cost to the high energy consumption.

exam.q: A student tests a sample of well water and finds it has a neutral pH of 7 and leaves a solid residue when boiled to dryness. Explain what this shows about the water.
model: The neutral pH shows it is not acidic or alkaline
The solid residue shows there are dissolved salts present
The water is potable (or safe to drink) but not chemically pure
exam.tip: Address both observations (pH and residue) to secure all 3 marks.

exam.q: Describe the purpose of adding chlorine during water treatment.
model: To kill microbes, bacteria, or harmful pathogens
exam.tip: One concise sentence mentioning sterilisation or killing bacteria gets the mark.

exam.q: In a school practical, a student heats 50 cm3 of a water sample in an evaporating basin until all the water has evaporated. The mass of the empty basin is 42.15 g, and the mass of the basin plus solid residue is 42.27 g. Calculate the mass of dissolved solids in the 50 cm3 sample.
exam.tip: Show your subtraction clearly: (mass with solid) - (empty mass).

exam.q: Explain how distillation removes dissolved sodium chloride from seawater.
model: Seawater is heated until water boils and turns into steam
Sodium chloride has a much higher boiling point so remains behind as solid residue
Steam is cooled and condensed back into pure liquid water in a condenser
exam.tip: Mention the fate of both the water (evaporates and condenses) and the salt (stays behind).

worked.q:
A student wants to determine the mass of dissolved solids in 25 cm3 of mineral water. They record the following data:
- Mass of empty evaporating basin = 35.40 g
- Mass of evaporating basin and dry solid residue = 35.64 g
Calculate the mass of dissolved solids per cm3 of mineral water.
steps: Identify the measured masses from the question.
Calculate the total mass of solid residue by subtracting the mass of the empty basin from the mass of the basin plus residue.
Divide the mass of the solid residue by the volume of water used (25 cm3) to find the mass per cm3.
worked.ans: Mass of solid = 35.64 g - 35.40 g = 0.24 g. Mass per cm3 = 0.24 g / 25 cm3 = 0.0096 g per cm3.

worked.q: Explain the stages involved in producing potable water from a reservoir containing acidic freshwater contaminated with suspended clay and bacteria.
steps: Address the suspended clay particles using filtration.
Address the bacteria and harmful microbes using sterilisation.
Address the acidity (if required to meet safe drinking standards) by neutralisation.
worked.ans: First, pass the water through sand and gravel filter beds to remove the insoluble suspended clay particles. Second, add chlorine gas or use UV light to sterilise the water and kill all harmful bacteria. Third, add a suitable neutralising agent or buffer if the acidity needs adjustment to meet potable pH standards.

chem_ocra.17.0.summary: The evolution of the Earth's atmosphere is a fascinating geological journey spanning 4.6 billion years. It transitioned from a toxic, volcanic gas-heavy environment dominated by carbon dioxide and water vapour into a stable, oxygen-rich atmosphere capable of supporting complex life, driven primarily by intense volcanic activity, the condensation of oceans, and the emergence of photosynthetic organisms.

core.h: First Billion Years and Intense Volcanic Activity
core.p: During the first billion years of Earth's existence, the surface was molten and extremely active. Intense volcanic activity released enormous volumes of gases into the young atmosphere, creating conditions completely unrecognisable to life today.
bullets: Earth's surface was initially molten with frequent volcanic eruptions.
Volcanoes released gases that formed the early atmosphere.
The primary gas released was carbon dioxide (CO2).
Significant amounts of water vapour (H2O) were also released.
Smaller proportions of methane (CH4), ammonia (NH3), and nitrogen (N2) were present.
Little to no free oxygen gas (O2) existed in this primordial phase.

callouts.p: The early atmosphere was largely similar to the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today, dominated by carbon dioxide.

core.h: Formation of the Oceans by Condensation
core.p: As the Earth slowly cooled down over millions of years, a critical phase change occurred that fundamentally altered the trajectory of planetary chemistry and allowed the formation of liquid water bodies.
bullets: The Earth's crust cooled sufficiently to allow water vapour to drop below its boiling point.
Water vapour condensed into liquid water as torrential rain over millions of years.
Water collected in hollows and basins in the Earth's crust to form the first oceans.
This massive liquid reservoir set the stage for subsequent chemical and biological processes.

callouts.p: The process where a gas turns into a liquid upon cooling.

core.h: Reduction of Carbon Dioxide via Oceans
core.p: The appearance of liquid oceans acted as a giant chemical sink, pulling massive quantities of carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere and permanently locking it away in geological formations.
bullets: Carbon dioxide is a highly water-soluble gas and dissolved readily into the newly formed oceans.
Dissolved CO2 reacted chemically with minerals dissolved in the water.
These reactions precipitated solid carbonate compounds, such as calcium carbonate.
Marine organisms later used these carbonates to build shells and skeletons (e.g., limestone formation).
When these organisms died, their remains settled to the ocean floor and formed sedimentary rocks over millions of years.

callouts.p: Do not just say CO2 'disappeared' into the oceans. Explain that it dissolved and then formed precipitates and sedimentary rocks.

core.h: Photosynthesis and the Rise of Oxygen
core.p: Once liquid oceans were established, primitive life evolved. Among the earliest life forms were photosynthetic organisms, which initiated a biological revolution by modifying the chemical composition of the entire planet.
bullets: Primitive algae and plants evolved in the oceans around 2.7 billion years ago.
These organisms carried out photosynthesis, absorbing carbon dioxide and water to produce glucose and oxygen.
Word equation: carbon dioxide + water -> glucose + oxygen.
Balanced symbol equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2.
Oxygen gas was slowly released as a waste product of photosynthesis into the oceans.
Once ocean water became saturated with oxygen, the gas bubbled out and began accumulating in the atmosphere.

callouts.p: The percentage of oxygen gradually increased over hundreds of millions of years, enabling the evolution of multicellular organisms and animals.

core.h: Rise of Nitrogen Gas Levels
core.p: Nitrogen is a very unreactive gas, which allowed its concentration in the atmosphere to build up and remain stable over geological timescales compared to volatile gases like carbon dioxide.
bullets: Volcanoes produced nitrogen gas in small amounts during early eruptions.
Nitrogen gas (N2) accumulated gradually because it is chemically inert and does not easily react with other substances.
Unlike carbon dioxide, nitrogen was not heavily absorbed by oceans or locked up rapidly in sedimentary rocks.
Denitrifying bacteria also released nitrogen into the atmosphere via the nitrogen cycle over long periods.
Today, nitrogen makes up approximately 78% of the Earth's atmosphere.

callouts.p: A gas that does not readily undergo chemical reactions with other elements or compounds due to a stable electronic structure.

core.h: Comparison of Past and Present Atmospheres
core.p: Examining the contrast between Earth's atmosphere 4 billion years ago and today reveals the dramatic impact of geological and biological processes.
bullets: Past atmosphere: Mostly CO2, high water vapour, traces of nitrogen, methane, ammonia, and zero oxygen.
Present atmosphere: 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.04% carbon dioxide, small variable amounts of water vapour, and about 0.9% argon.
The shift shows a massive reduction in CO2 and a massive increase in O2 and N2.

core.h: Role of Fossil Fuels in Locking Up Carbon
core.p: Biological carbon sequestration did not stop with carbonate rocks; living matter itself played a major role in removing carbon dioxide from the active carbon cycle.
bullets: Plants and microscopic marine organisms (plankton) photosynthesised and absorbed carbon dioxide.
When these organisms died, they fell to the seabed or were buried in swamps under anaerobic conditions.
Over millions of years, heat and pressure converted these buried organic remains into fossil fuels (coal, crude oil, and natural gas).
This process effectively trapped carbon underground for millions of years, maintaining low atmospheric CO2 levels until human extraction began.

callouts.p: Always link the formation of coal, crude oil, and natural gas to the burial of dead biomass over geological timescales.

core.h: Ammonia and Methane Breakdown
core.p: The primordial atmosphere contained significant amounts of reducing gases like ammonia and methane, which were eventually removed through atmospheric chemical reactions.
bullets: Methane (CH4) and ammonia (NH3) were released by early volcanic activity.
As oxygen levels began to rise due to early photosynthesis, methane reacted with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water.
Ammonia reacted with early oxygen to produce nitrogen gas and water vapour.
These reactions removed almost all of the primordial methane and ammonia from the atmosphere.

callouts.p: The rise of oxygen acted as an oxidising agent that destroyed atmospheric methane and ammonia.

core.h: Timeline of Atmospheric Evolution
core.p: Understanding the sequence of events is crucial for sequencing questions in the exam. The timeline is divided into distinct geological phases.
bullets: Phase 1 (4.6 to 3.5 billion years ago): Volcanic outgassing produces mainly CO2, H2O vapour, and N2.
Phase 2 (3.5 to 2.7 billion years ago): Oceans form by condensation; CO2 dissolves into oceans and forms carbonate rocks.
Phase 3 (2.7 billion years ago onwards): Algae and plants evolve and perform photosynthesis, raising O2 levels significantly.
Phase 4 (Present day): Dynamic equilibrium established with 78% N2, 21% O2, and trace gases.

core.h: Limitations of Scientific Evidence
core.p: Because the evolution of the Earth's atmosphere occurred billions of years ago, scientists rely on indirect evidence, meaning theories are continuously tested and refined as new data emerges.
bullets: Direct sampling of the atmosphere 4 billion years ago is impossible.
Evidence is gathered from gas bubbles trapped in ancient ice cores, sedimentary rock layers, and chemical fingerprints in ancient minerals (like zircons).
The time scale is so vast that exact rates of gas emission and absorption remain estimates subject to revision.
Peer review and new analytical techniques allow scientists to build increasingly accurate models.

callouts.p: A cylinder of ice drilled from an ice sheet, containing trapped air bubbles that preserve ancient atmospheric samples.

analogy.t: The Planet as a Brewing Pot of Soup
analogy.p: Imagine the early Earth as a giant, sealed pot of boiling vegetable soup over a roaring fire (volcanoes). At first, the pot is full of heavy steam and pungent vapours (water vapour and carbon dioxide). As the burner is turned down and the pot cools, the steam condenses and drips down the sides into a liquid broth at the bottom (forming the oceans). Later, microscopic bacteria are dropped into the broth, bubbling away and slowly pumping fresh oxygen into the air space under the lid until the mixture resembles a clean, breathable environment. Where the analogy breaks down: the real Earth is an open system exposed to space, and geological time scales are millions of times longer than cooking soup.

terms.d: The release of gases trapped in the Earth's interior into the atmosphere through volcanic eruptions.
The phase change of water vapour into liquid water as temperature drops below the boiling point.
Endothermic chemical process where plants use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to produce glucose and oxygen.
Rock formed by the accumulation, compaction, and cementation of mineral particles or organic matter over time.
A sedimentary rock primarily composed of calcium carbonate, formed from the skeletal remains of marine organisms.
Natural fuels such as coal, crude oil, and natural gas formed from the remains of living organisms over millions of years.
The long-term storage of carbon dioxide or other forms of carbon to mitigate global warming.
A gas that does not undergo chemical reactions under normal conditions due to a stable outer electron shell.
Simple, plant-like aquatic organisms that were among the earliest life forms to perform photosynthesis.
An insoluble solid formed by a chemical reaction in a solution.
A state of balance where the rates of gas production and gas removal from the atmosphere roughly equal each other.
A core sample from an ice sheet used to reconstruct historical atmospheric composition and temperature.

mistakes.w: Oxygen was the most abundant gas in the early atmosphere.
mistakes.r: Oxygen was virtually absent in the early atmosphere; carbon dioxide was the most abundant gas.

mistakes.w: Oceans formed because comets brought all the water and it stayed as liquid instantly.
mistakes.r: Water vapour was released by volcanoes and condensed as the Earth cooled down sufficiently.

mistakes.w: Carbon dioxide just vanished into thin air.
mistakes.r: Carbon dioxide dissolved in oceans, reacted to form precipitates, and was locked up in sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels.

mistakes.w: Plants created nitrogen in the atmosphere.
mistakes.r: Nitrogen accumulated because it is an unreactive gas released by volcanoes and not rapidly removed.

mistakes.w: The atmosphere has always had 21% oxygen.
mistakes.r: Oxygen only began to accumulate around 2.7 billion years ago due to photosynthesis by algae and plants.

mistakes.w: Methane and ammonia increased over time.
mistakes.r: Methane and ammonia reacted with newly formed oxygen and were destroyed.

mistakes.w: Volcanoes released large amounts of oxygen gas.
mistakes.r: Volcanoes released carbon dioxide, water vapour, nitrogen, methane, and ammonia, but little to no oxygen.

exam.q: Give two gases that were released by volcanic activity in the early Earth's atmosphere.
model: Carbon dioxide
Water vapour (or methane, ammonia, nitrogen)
exam.tip: State any two valid gases from the accepted list. Do not write oxygen.

exam.q: Explain how the formation of oceans helped decrease the amount of carbon dioxide in the Earth's atmosphere.
model: Carbon dioxide dissolved in the water of the newly formed oceans
Dissolved carbon dioxide reacted with metal ions to form precipitates
These precipitates formed sedimentary carbonate rocks over millions of years
exam.tip: Include both the dissolving step and the rock formation step for full marks.

exam.q: Write a word equation for photosynthesis.
model: Carbon dioxide + water -> glucose + oxygen
exam.tip: Ensure you use an arrow (->) and not an equals sign.

exam.q: Describe and explain how the percentage of oxygen in the atmosphere changed from 3 billion years ago to the present day.
model: Oxygen percentage was zero 3 billion years ago
Algae and plants evolved and began carrying out photosynthesis
Photosynthesis absorbs carbon dioxide and produces oxygen
Oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere, reaching about 21% today
exam.tip: Mention algae/plants and photosynthesis to score the biological mechanism marks.

exam.q: Explain why scientists do not have exact, definitive proof of the Earth's atmosphere composition 4 billion years ago.
model: It happened billions of years ago and humans were not present to record it
Evidence is indirect and based on analysis of rocks, fossils, or ice cores which can be interpreted in different ways
exam.tip: Focus on the time elapsed and the reliance on indirect evidence.

exam.q: State the current approximate percentages of nitrogen and oxygen in the Earth's atmosphere.
model: Nitrogen: approximately 78%
Oxygen: approximately 21%
exam.tip: Learn these percentages precisely as examiners frequently test them.

exam.q: Explain why the proportion of nitrogen gas in the atmosphere increased over time.
model: Nitrogen was released by volcanic activity and produced by biological processes
Nitrogen is a very unreactive (inert) gas so it was not removed quickly by chemical or physical reactions
exam.tip: Emphasise that nitrogen's lack of reactivity (inertness) is why it built up and stayed in the air.

exam.q: Describe what happened to the methane and ammonia that were present in the early atmosphere.
model: They reacted with the oxygen produced by photosynthesis
Methane was oxidised to carbon dioxide and water; ammonia was oxidised to nitrogen and water
exam.tip: Link their disappearance directly to the arrival of oxygen gas.

exam.q: Outline how fossil fuels (such as coal) contributed to reducing atmospheric carbon dioxide.
model: Plants and trees absorbed carbon dioxide via photosynthesis
When these plants died, they were buried in swampy wetlands under anaerobic conditions
Over millions of years, pressure and heat converted them into coal, locking up the carbon underground
exam.tip: Mention burial and lack of oxygen (anaerobic conditions) for the geological process.

worked.q: A student analyses a sample of gas from a volcanic vent. It contains 82% carbon dioxide, 12% water vapour, 4% nitrogen, and 2% sulfur dioxide. Explain how this data supports the theory of the early Earth's atmosphere.
steps: Identify the primary gases in the sample: carbon dioxide and water vapour make up the vast majority (94%).
Relate this high proportion of greenhouse/volcanic gases to Phase 1 of atmospheric evolution where intense volcanic outgassing dominated.
Note the low concentration of oxygen and nitrogen, matching the scientific model that early Earth lacked free oxygen.
worked.ans: The sample is dominated by carbon dioxide and water vapour, which aligns with the theory that early Earth's atmosphere was formed by intense volcanic outgassing releasing large quantities of these gases while lacking free oxygen.

worked.q: Calculate the total percentage of gases in the modern atmosphere if nitrogen is 78.08%, oxygen is 20.95%, argon is 0.93%, and carbon dioxide is 0.04%. State what the remaining trace gases make up.
steps: State that the remaining trace gases make up 0% beyond these specified values, or note that other noble gases make up the tiny remainder if rounding is applied.
worked.ans: Total = 78.08 + 20.95 + 0.93 + 0.04 = 100.00%. The specified gases account for 100% of the dry clean air composition.

svg.cap: Figure 1: Evolution of the Earth's atmosphere showing the decline of carbon dioxide and the rise of oxygen over geological time.
svg.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="0" y="0" width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><line x1="50" y1="200" x2="370" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="30" x2="50" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="180" y="225" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">Time (Billions of Years Ago)</text><text x="10" y="115" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12" transform="rotate(-90 10 115)">Percentage (%)</text><path d="M50 50 Q 150 70, 350 180" fill="none" stroke="#ef4444" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M50 190 Q 200 185, 350 60" fill="none" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="50" cy="50" r="4" fill="#ef4444"/><circle cx="350" cy="180" r="4" fill="#ef4444"/><circle cx="50" cy="190" r="4" fill="#3b82f6"/><circle cx="350" cy="60" r="4" fill="#3b82f6"/><text x="200" y="90" fill="#ef4444" font-size="12">Carbon dioxide (decreases)</text><text x="150" y="130" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="12">Oxygen (increases)</text><text x="45" y="215" fill="#1b2540" font-size="11">4.6</text><text x="200" y="215" fill="#1b2540" font-size="11">2.5</text><text x="350" y="215" fill="#1b2540" font-size="11">0</text></svg>

svg.cap: Figure 2: Summary of processes that removed carbon dioxide from the early atmosphere and locked it into the Earth.
